 Inside Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4: The New Game-Changing Tech Powering Every Mode 
 Smoke, weather and animation have all seen huge upgrades.
 by William Judd 
 Yesterday, 3:21pm 
 Share:
 Subscribe to Digital Foundry on YouTube 1.5m 
 Here's the full behind-the-scenes video from Krakow, featuring Tom and Infinity Ward Poland studio head (and principal rendering engineer) Michal Drobot. 
 Infinity Ward recently opened its Krakow research and development centre to us to showcase the technical advancements powering Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4. Infinity Ward Poland studio head Michal Drobot was on hand to present debug footage that explained how current-gen hardware on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S and PC enables unprecedented visual and systemic upgrades. While a Nintendo Switch 2 version is also launching in parallel via Digital Legends, the core engine focus remains firmly on pushing broader performance and graphical boundaries - including ray-marched smoke and fog, revamped rasterisation techniques informed by path tracing, and a comprehensively reworked animation and movement system.
 Let's start with one of the standout additions, a brand new volumetric ray-marched smoke and fog system built exclusively for MW4. Working in tandem with traditional transparencies, this voxel-based solution allows players to interact directly with smoke plumes using gunfire or vehicles. Bullets carve precise temporary holes through the volume - as in Counter-Strike 2 - while sprinting characters displace wisps naturally, all operating within a fixed GPU performance ceiling.
 This unified voxel framework extends seamlessly across atmospheric elements, height fog, and overhead clouds, ensuring consistent competitive balance across all online multiplayer and DMZ modes. Server and local client synchronisation guarantees that visual interactions such as lighting, shadows, and smoke dispersion appear identically for every participant. Furthermore, volumetric fog self shadows and interacts dynamically with animated light sources within the environment.
 Here are debug shots from the game's production showing volumetric fog (left, centre left) and voxels (centre right, right). Click to enlarge. 
 Weather systems also benefit heavily from the new voxel architecture, supporting dynamic transitions between sunshine, rainfall and snow across expansive open maps - a huge change for open-ended modes like DMZ. Snow layers accumulate dynamically on top of existing level geometry, allowing players to gradually reveal the original terrain beneath. Additionally, expanded character and object voxels now track more environmental states than previous games - a great range of variables that coats soldiers in mud, dust, blood or water streaks depending on their movement.
 Next there's the new material workflow used in Modern Warfare 4. While full path tracing is reserved for internal visual reference only due to its heavy performance cost - and RT global illumination and RT reflections are PC-exclusive features - MW4 developers chose to heavily optimise rasterisation pipelines, achieving visual results remarkably close to path tracing at a fraction of the computational expense. This strategy ensures the game easily maintains a high frame-rate across a much wider spectrum of hardware, a key consideration given how much of Call of Duty's audience plays on console with 60fps in mind.
 Here's how a frame is affected by screen space elements - including SSA (screen space ambient occlusion), SSBN (screen-space bent normals), and SSGI (screen-space global illumination). Click to enlarge. 
 A core component of this improved rasterised approach is the neural light grid, which leverages machine learning compression to handle dynamic ambient occlusion and global illumination, a rethought approach that seeks to avoid the typical artefacts caused by screen-space reflections (SSR) and screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO). By storing lighting data more efficiently, light probes can be distributed sparsely across levels without sacrificing visual fidelity. Incidentally, it's an innovation that also helps to reduce the game's installation sizes alongside improved texture streaming techniques.
 In part, material rendering receives a major upgrade through custom capture hardware known as the ATVI CT Reflectometer 2.0. By capturing physical surface properties across multiple light gradients, artists are able to access accurate bidirectional reflectance distribution function values for skin, clothing and metallic surfaces. This new material workflow integrates well with the enhanced rasterised ambient occlusion and global illumination passes.
 Under the hood, significant optimisations target the entire rendering pipeline through advanced variable rate shading. Variable rate shading dynamically compresses visual data in less critical areas while preserving full native resolution where it matters most, drastically reducing overall graphical overhead - and this time, it's now applied throughout the entire render pipeline, not just for the final rendered pixels. Additional efficiency is gained through multi-resolution transparencies, with effects like smoke scaling in resolution based on distance.
 Screenshots of MW4 using raster techniques, ray-traced global illumination and path tracing. The latter is used only as a reference material for artists, while RTGI is available as an option on PC. Click to enlarge. 
 Supporting these techniques, a hybrid rendering setup is also in place: combining traditional forward rendering (F+) with a visibility buffer (V+) for dense geometry. Where it's efficient to do so, parts of the scene will flip from one to the other, with F+ tending to handle triangles nearer the player.
 Finally, foundational gameplay mechanics have been completely overhauled alongside these more visual-focused upgrades. Character movement directly influences weapon sway and contextual interactions with walls, while a new physical bullet trajectory simulation replaces older random bloom mechanics.
 Together with these technical engineering achievements, Modern Warfare 4 stands as one of the more significant series milestones. It refines the experience for long term fans of the franchise - and impressions from the early access period suggest the campaign at least is one of the series' best in recent memory. We'll have more to say on Modern Warfare 4 to come, including the Switch 2 edition, but for now the outlook on the game's tech is promising to say the least.
